They can transmit pathogens uncommon here, including Rickettsia and Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus; all known cases were imported, but establishment is a concern. The forest/marsh tick is spreading and can carry Tibola syndrome and babesiosis; babesiosis affects humans and is dangerous for dogs. A University of Zurich project collected over 10,000 ticks from 16 hosts to map circulating pathogens. Climate warming expands tick habitat to 2000 m and lengthens activity; April 2026 was the fifth-warmest on record, with FSME at 43 cases by end-April (0.5/100,000).

articleSummary: Chagas disease, a neglected tropical infection, affects up to 6 million people worldwide, mostly in Latin America, and can remain silent for decades before causing irreversible heart damage. Transmission traditionally occurs via Triatomine kissing bugs at night, when defecation containing Trypanosoma cruzi is introduced to bite wounds or mucous membranes. In recent decades, transmission via blood transfusions, organ transplants, contaminated foods or drinks, and mother-to-child transmission has grown; in Brazil, oral transmission through contaminated fruit juice now accounts for over half of acute cases. About 30% of infected individuals develop severe cardiomyopathy, arrhythmias, stroke, or heart failure many years post-infection. Diagnosis is rare and often incidental; in many countries fewer than 10% of infections are diagnosed, and in Latin America perhaps 10–20%. Early treatment with benznidazole or nifurtimox is highly effective, but the therapeutic window is often missed. The WHO notes Chagas is present in 44 countries, including the United States and Europe, reflecting a growing risk due to migration.

Persistence in semen up to 15 months after recovery.

Ituri Province accounts for about 95% of DRC cases; infections also reported in North Kivu and South Kivu. Sixteen healthcare workers in the DRC have been infected. In Uganda, most cases are in Kampala and Wakiso, linked to travelers from Congo or contacts; sustained community transmission in Uganda is not reported, though hundreds of contacts are under monitoring. Bundibugyo virus disease is zoonotic (fruit bats are likely reservoir); transmission occurs via direct contact with infected fluids or contaminated materials and in healthcare settings without proper IPC. Early symptoms include fever, fatigue, headache, and muscle pain; severe disease can cause organ failure and hemorrhage. Historical fatality rates range 30–50%, with current rate under investigation. More than 5,000 contacts are monitored in the DRC and nearly 700 in Uganda. Response includes surveillance, contact tracing, laboratory strengthening, IPC, and risk communication; cross-border surveillance and coordination are emphasized; no travel restrictions advised. Risk: very high in the DRC, high in Uganda and neighboring countries.

articleSummary: Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak declared in DRC's Ituri Province on 15 May 2026; the WHO declared a Public Health Emergency of International Concern on 16–17 May, with Africa CDC declaring an emergency the next day. By June, hundreds of cases and over a hundred deaths were reported, confined to the DRC and Uganda, with imported cases including health-worker deaths in Kampala. Transmission requires direct contact with blood or body fluids of a symptomatic or deceased patient, not airborne. Lagos, Nigeria emphasizes preparedness through surveillance, emergency operations center, border biosecurity, lab diagnosis, and contact tracing under Nigeria's IDSR framework, monitoring Lassa, cholera, measles, mpox, and Ebola.
